extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or graduate students and scholars of American government and constitutional law
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of constitutional limits on state power (contract clause, Fourteenth Amendment limits, police power, admission of states, and state constitutional structure), with leading cases and examples illustrating judicial tests and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on ex post facto and retrospective criminal legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: States may not pass laws that make an act criminal which was not criminal when committed, or change rules of evidence so that different or less testimony is sufficient to convict than was required when the deed was committed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limitation was designed to protect citizens from punishment by legislative acts having retrospective operation, and applies only to criminal legislation. (Discussion references werking of ex post facto prohibitions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract Clause — no law impairing obligation of contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution provides that no state shall pass any law impairing the obligation of contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'contract' is used broadly: 'a legally binding agreement in respect to property, either expressed or implied, executory or executed, between private parties, or between a commonwealth and a private party or parties; or a grant from one party to another; or a grant, charter, or franchise, from a commonwealth to a private party or private parties.' This broad interpretation has been applied to protect corporate franchises, charters, and privileges (e.g., Dartmouth College, Bank of Ohio v. Knoop).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract Clause — retrospective application requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A state law will be invalid under the Contract Clause only when it is retrospective — i.e., when it applies to contracts made before its passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a state provides in its constitution or laws for future revision of charters, franchises, and other forms of contract, it thereby places the right to alter the terms of new grants within the body of the law, avoiding impairment. Many states include provisions allowing alteration or repeal of corporate acts after passage to prevent perpetual entrenchment of privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on what counts as a 'contract' under the clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain agreements between a state and its citizens have been held not to be 'contracts' for Contract Clause purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: appointment to a public office for a definite term at fixed salary is not a contract (state may abolish the office); grants of power to municipal corporations, bounty laws promising payments on production, and state licenses for selling liquor for a term are not treated as contracts in this context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileges and Immunities Clause (Fourteenth Amendment) — scope debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1: 'no state shall make or enforce any law which may abridge the privileges or immunities of citizens of the United States.' There is debate over whether this nationalizes all civil liberties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The nationalist view argues it nationalizes the liberties guaranteed against the federal government (first ten amendments); the Supreme Court rejected that broad reading and adopted a narrow interpretation, enumerating a limited set of privileges (access to federal functions, seaports/sub-treasuries/land offices/courts, habeas corpus, use of navigable waters, peaceable assembly and petition). The Court's narrow construction limits the clause's applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due Process Clause (Fourteenth Amendment) — substantive scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1 forbids a state to deprive any person of life, liberty, or property without due process of law; 'life' extends beyond mere existence; 'liberty' is freedom to act within lawfully imposed limits; 'property' includes every form of vested right legally acquired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court has refused to define 'due process' abstractly; instead it examines its meaning through judicial decisions and application to classes of state laws. Due process is informed by 'the law of the land' (state law) and by immutable principles of free government as understood by the judiciary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process in criminal cases (procedural flexibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Fourteenth Amendment, due process in criminal cases does not necessarily require replication of all processes in the Bill of Rights (e.g., grand jury indictment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hurtado v. California held that indictment by grand jury is not required under the Fourteenth Amendment; due process may be satisfied by other legal proceedings (e.g., prosecution by information) so long as the proceedings preserve core principles of liberty and justice and are in furtherance of the public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process in civil cases (notice and judicial proceedings)
rubrics_metrics.description: For civil matters, due process is met if trials are held according to the established course of judicial proceedings, providing reasonable security, full notice, and satisfactory protection to persons involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Walker v. Sauvinet held trial by jury is not a privilege states are forbidden to abridge under the Fourteenth Amendment; what matters is that the process affords adequate procedural protections (notice, opportunity to be heard, judicial process).

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process in taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a tax is imposed according to valuation of property, due process requires general notice to the owner and a hearing for complaints so the owner may contest liability; personal notice is not necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By contrast, the right to be heard is not a necessary part of due process for poll and license taxes, specific taxes fixed by legislative enactment, or many other taxes definitively set by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process and administrative/judicial review (corporations/commissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: State action that deprives parties of judicial investigation or substitutes absolute administrative finality without judicial review may violate due process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a Minnesota statute empowering a railway commission to fix rates without provision for judicial review was held unconstitutional because it deprived a railway company of its right to judicial investigation into matters in controversy. The Court treats access to judicial machinery for review as part of due process in many contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process versus economic regulation (liberty to contract)
rubrics_metrics.description: State regulations affecting labor and contracts can be invalidated if they are unreasonable, unnecessary, and arbitrary interferences with the liberty to contract — a liberty protected by the Fourteenth Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: New York law limiting bakery employees to sixty hours a week and ten hours a day was held invalid as an unreasonable interference with the right and liberty to contract. However, courts require state regulations (e.g., rate regulation) to be 'reasonable' and to allow proper returns on investment where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police power — permissible state interference with life, liberty, property
rubrics_metrics.description: States may, under 'police power,' enact regulations to promote health, peace, morals, education, good order, and general welfare, which may interfere with life, liberty, and property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court refuses to rigidly define 'police power,' reserving to itself the right to judge whether particular acts are warranted. Concrete examples of permissible police power actions include restricting dangerous trades to localities, confining the insane or persons with contagious diseases, limited regulation of railways and common carriers, and ordering destruction of buildings endangering public safety. The scope depends on judicial social and political theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal regulatory encroachment on state autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Growth of national industries, interstate commerce, and national business organizations increases federal regulatory authority and reduces state autonomy over certain matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulation of interstate interests is confided to the federal government, which expands supervisory activities; federal courts take jurisdiction over suits between citizens of different states, increasing federal influence in matters once controlled by states (examples: Interstate Commerce Commission supervision of rates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission of new states — constitutional basics and process
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution allows new states to be admitted by Congress; no new state may be formed out of another state or by junction of parts of states without consent of legislatures and Congress. Ordinary process: petition by inhabitants, enabling act, territorial convention to frame constitution, compliance, congressional resolution declaring statehood, executive proclamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods have varied historically (e.g., Texas admitted as independent republic by Congress; California admitted without territorial stage). Congress has sometimes delayed admission pending suggested amendments to territorial constitutions (Missouri, Kansas, Utah, Oklahoma).

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional conditions on admission and equality of states
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether Congress may impose limitations on a state admitted to the Union beyond the federal Constitution's requirements; theory holds all states admitted are equal in rights and privileges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Northwest Ordinance declared new states admitted 'on an equal footing' with original states. The Supreme Court has said territorial limitations cease to be operative unless voluntarily adopted by the state after admission, yet in some cases the Court has upheld certain limitations (particularly property-related) imposed at admission (examples: Minnesota, Nevada enabling act conditions). The Court distinguishes political/power limitations from property-related agreements between a state and the nation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to draft state constitutions subject to federal limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject to federal Constitutional limitations and any limitations at admission, the voters of each state may draft their state's constitution as they please.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite theoretical freedom, striking similarities exist among state constitutions, often reflecting historical periods. Conventions drafting constitutions frequently use comparative compilations of other states' provisions; newer constitutions often borrow clauses from others. States commonly structure constitutions into standard parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical structural parts of a state constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: A state constitution usually falls into six parts: (1) a bill of rights; (2) sections providing the framework of government (central and local) and fundamental limitations of each branch; (3) sections dealing with state finances; (4) clauses for control of economic interests (railways, insurance, banking, labor); (5) clauses providing for education and social welfare; (6) the amendment clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taxonomy helps compare constitutions and locate where particular rights or regulations are commonly placed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents of state bills of rights — traditional guarantees
rubrics_metrics.description: State bills of rights commonly include ancient protections: indictment by grand jury; trial by jury; free exercise of religion; habeas corpus (except in rebellion/invasion/public danger); prohibition of excessive bail/fines and cruel and unusual punishments; compensation for private property taken for public use; free speech/press subject to libel responsibility; right to assemble and petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alongside these traditional guarantees, many state constitutions (especially recent ones) add new provisions or modify procedures (for example, provisioning prosecution by information in some jurisdictions while preserving other protections).
